For each seed user: find other tweets mentioning topic keyword -> extract phrasal patterns by replacing topic with variable A (node: candidate patterns)
Manual ranking and filtering of patterns -> select top 100 pro / top 100 con patterns (node: curated patterns)
Apply curated patterns to entire tweet corpus -> collect (u,t,+1/-1) instances (node: raw tuples; evidence: 25.8M then filtered to 9.96M)
Aggregate counts to compute ru,t = (#pro - #con)/(#pro + #con) for observed (u,t) (node: sparse R matrix)
Optimize low-rank factorization on observed entries of R (libmf) -> obtain P (user vectors) and Q (topic vectors) (node: latent space)
Use puᵀqt to (i) predict sign(r̂u,t) for held-out known entries and (ii) compute cosine similarities between topic vectors to propose inter-topic preferences (node: downstream tasks)

Evaluate (i) prediction accuracy stratified by user vocality (θ thresholds) and (ii) inter-topic similarity against crowdsourced labels (Spearman ρ=0.221), plus qualitative nearest-neighbor topic lists (node: empirical evidence)

Conclusions: (a) pattern-seeded extraction scales and yields large R, (b) MF can complete missing stances for many users (esp. those with some known preferences), (c) topic vectors encode meaningful inter-topic preference structure beyond a single axis (k>1 needed)

identified_claims.claim_text: High-quality linguistic patterns extracted from hashtag-bearing tweets can be used to collect large-scale user-topic preference tuples (u, t, v) indicating pro/con stances.
evidence: Regexes for pro and con hashtags (#(.+)sansei, #(.+)hantai) and extraction procedure (Sec. 2.1).
31,068 occurrences of pro/con hashtags from 18,582 users for 4,899 topics (Sec. 2.1).
After filtering, 9,961,509 tuples for 273,417 users and 2,323 topics (Sec. 2.2).
Manual selection of top 100 pro and top 100 con patterns (Sec. 2.1).
uncertainty_flags: No reported precision/recall or sampled accuracy of pattern matches; manual filtering steps introduce opaque selection bias.
Hashtag morphology / conventions are language-specific (Japanese), limiting direct transfer.

identified_claims.claim_text: User-topic preference values ru,t can be computed as (#pro - #con)/(#pro + #con) from extracted instances, producing values in [-1,+1] that represent degree of expressed preference.
evidence: Equation 1 defines ru,t = (#(u,t,+1) - #(u,t,-1)) / (#(u,t,+1) + #(u,t,-1)).
uncertainty_flags: No smoothing or variance estimation for low-count cells; single-instance ru,t = ±1 is fragile.
Temporal dynamics and sarcasm/negation are not modeled, so ru,t may mix noise with signal.

identified_claims.claim_text: Modeling the sparse user-topic matrix with low-rank matrix factorization yields user and topic latent vectors that can predict missing user-topic preferences with high accuracy (~82–94% depending on known preferences).
evidence: Libmf used to factorize R excluding missing entries (Section 3).
Evaluation: random 5% held-out elements; accuracy measured by sign agreement (Equation 5, Sec. 4.2).
Reported accuracy: 82.1% for users with ≥5 known topics; 94.0% for ≥100 known topics (Figure 3).
uncertainty_flags: Held-out evaluation removes known entries but does not test zero-shot for users with no observed topics or new topics.
No multiple-run statistics (CI, p-values) reported; potential selection/retraining leakage not fully specified.

identified_claims.claim_text: Latent topic vectors capture meaningful inter-topic preference relations (those who agree A also tend to agree B), supported by qualitative nearest-neighbor examples and a positive Spearman correlation (ρ=0.221) with crowd judgments.
evidence: Crowdsourced dataset of 450 topic pairs sampled by cosine-similarity ranges; 6–10 judgments per pair, worker filtering with 20 gold pairs (Sec. 4.3).
Spearman’s ρ between cosine similarity and averaged human judgments reported as 0.221.
Qualitative lists of similar topics for LDP, constitutional amendment, and foreigners' voting rights (Table 2).
uncertainty_flags: Correlation is modest (ρ=0.221) leaving most variance unexplained.
Crowdsourcing instruction details, inter-annotator agreement, and label calibration not fully reported; sampling by model score can bias results.

identified_claims.claim_text: A multi-dimensional latent space (k>1; chosen k=100) is necessary; a single liberal–conservative axis is insufficient to represent the diversity of topic preferences.
evidence: RMSE decreases with increasing k; k=1 yields higher RMSE (Figure 2).
Authors select k=100 as sufficient for reconstruction and use it in downstream experiments (Sec. 4.1).
uncertainty_flags: Model selection for k lacks held-out validation on downstream tasks (prediction accuracy or correlation) and no overfitting checks.
RMSE improvement may continue beyond k=100; computational/regularization trade-offs not documented.

identified_claims.claim_label: approach fills gap for ordinary users
identified_claims.claim_text: The matrix factorization approach helps complete preferences for less vocal ('ordinary') users, bridging gap between vocal and ordinary users in stance coverage.
identified_claims.section_anchor: Sections 1 and 4.2 (Introduction; Predicting missing topic preferences)
evidence: Cites Cohen & Ruths (2013) about difficulty with ordinary users; the paper shows prediction accuracy improves with more known preferences and argues MF completes missing entries (Sec. 4.2).
Figure 4 shows mean variance of ru,t increases with user vocality, suggesting vocal users deviate from average.
uncertainty_flags: No direct evaluation on truly ordinary users (e.g., cold-start users with zero observations); generalization depends on representativeness of training users.
Latent factors learned from vocal users may not transfer to ordinary users if missingness is non-random.

strengths.title: Large-scale, real-world dataset construction
strengths.description: The authors assemble a very large Japanese Twitter-derived stance dataset (≈9.96M extracted tuples over 273k users and 2.3k topics) enabling empirical study at scale.
evidence: Initial extraction: 25,805,909 tuples -> filtered to 9,961,509 tuples; 273,417 users and 2,323 topics (Section 2.2).

strengths.title: Clear, operational pipeline from seeds to latent space
strengths.description: Paper gives a reconstructable pipeline: hashtag seeds -> pattern mining -> pattern curation -> instance extraction -> ru,t aggregation -> libmf factorization; this makes replication feasible with provided parameter choices.
evidence: Detailed description of regex seeds, manual ranking procedure, ru,t formula (Eq.1), objective (Eq.2), libmf use and λ settings (Section 3).

strengths.title: Empirical demonstration of utility for stance completion
strengths.description: Sign-prediction evaluation stratified by user vocality shows MF meaningfully improves completion, with accuracy rising with available signals (82.1% -> 94.0%).
evidence: Figure 3 and Section 4.2 report accuracy numbers for thresholds θ and comparison with majority baseline.

strengths.title: Thoughtful discussion of limitations and future work
strengths.description: Authors explicitly list assumptions and pathways for future improvements (fine-grained opinion analysis, causality), indicating awareness of boundaries and reasonable next steps.
evidence: Section 5 discusses fine-grained opinion analysis and causality; several explicit assumptions are described in Section 2.1.

concerns.title: No reported precision / recall or sampled error analysis for extracted (u,t,v) tuples
concerns.description: The paper omits empirical estimates of extraction quality (false positive rate, false negative patterns) and common error modes (sarcasm, negation, topical ambiguity), making ru,t and downstream factorization vulnerable to unquantified noise.
evidence: Shared analysis notes: no automatic precision/recall numbers reported; manual pattern selection; ru,t may be affected by false positives (Section 2.1–2.2).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Randomly sample extracted (u,t,v) tuples (stratified by topic frequency and by pro/con) and report precision; sample negative cases to estimate recall; annotate typical failure modes (sarcasm, negation, quoting). Provide these numbers in a new table and consider automatic filters or weak supervision to reduce noise.

concerns.title: ru,t computation is brittle for low-count cells and ignores temporal dynamics
concerns.description: The normalized-count ru,t = (#+ - #-) / (#+ + #-) produces extreme ±1 values from one-off matches; no smoothing, uncertainty measures, or temporal modeling provided.
evidence: Equation 1 defines ru,t without smoothing; authors remove users/topics with <5 occurrences but many remain with low counts (Section 3, 2.2).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Introduce Bayesian smoothing (e.g., add-α or Beta posterior mean), report distribution of counts per observed ru,t, and run sensitivity analysis (prediction and topic-cosine correlation) under alternative ru,t transforms (smoothed ratio, logit of counts, count-weighted loss).

concerns.title: Evaluation protocol lacks uncertainty quantification and broader generalization checks
concerns.description: Prediction evaluation uses a single random 5% held-out of observed entries and reports point estimates without confidence intervals, cross-validation, or experiments on cold-start users/topics.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes 5% held-out and reports accuracies but does not provide CIs, multiple runs, or cold-start tests.
Shared analysis flags missing statistical details and leakage concerns.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Repeat experiments with multiple random seeds / folds, report standard errors or 95% CIs, include a cold-start evaluation (users with zero training observations) and leave-one-topic-out for topics to test generalization, and clarify train/test construction to rule out leakage.

concerns.title: Model selection for k and regularization is under-justified
concerns.description: k is chosen by inspecting RMSE curve (authors select k=100) but without held-out validation on downstream tasks (prediction accuracy or topic-judgment correlation) or reporting overfitting behavior for large k.
evidence: Section 4.1: RMSE decreases with k; authors state k=100 is sufficient but provide no validation-based selection.
Shared analysis suggests lacking rigorous model-selection evidence.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Use a validation set (distinct from test Y) to choose k by optimizing downstream metrics (prediction accuracy and correlation with human judgments), report performance vs k for those metrics, and include regularization hyperparameter search with reported results.

concerns.title: Interpretation of topic-vector cosine as inter-topic preference is ambiguous
concerns.description: Cosine similarity may reflect topical/semantic co-occurrence or frequency artifacts, not necessarily the preference relationships the paper intends; crowd correlation is modest (ρ=0.221) and sampling topic pairs by cosine may bias the evaluation.
evidence: Section 4.3: sampling stratified on cosine (below -0.6, between, above 0.6), then computing Spearman ρ=0.221.
Assumption A7/A8 in shared analysis: cosine and stratified sampling may confound signals.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Complement cosine-based evaluation with alternative baselines (e.g., conditional co-occurrence PMI of pro statements, raw co-occurrence of users who express both topics with same sign, and supervised classifier of inter-topic association). Report inter-annotator agreement on crowd labels and rerun correlation with an evaluation set sampled uniformly at random (not stratified by model score).

concerns.title: Language- and hashtag-specific design limits external validity
concerns.description: The pipeline leverages Japanese hashtag morphology (sansei/hantai). The assumption that these seeds generalize to other languages/platforms is untested and may fail where hashtag conventions differ.
evidence: Paper explicitly uses Japanese corpus and notes patterns are language specific (Section 2.1).
Shared analysis: dataset is Japanese-specific; transfer unverified (Assumption A10).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Demonstrate portability by applying the pipeline to a small English Twitter sample using English equivalents (e.g., #pro<topic>, #anti<topic> or curated hashtag lists), or at minimum discuss methods to adapt seeding for other languages and evaluate on a held-out non-Japanese subset.

concerns.title: Manual pattern curation introduces opaque bias and reduces reproducibility
concerns.description: Sorting by user-frequency and manual removal of 'unuseful' patterns is not reproducible and may bias patterns toward frequent, possibly idiosyncratic phrasing.
evidence: Section 2.1: manual selection of top 100 pro and top 100 con patterns after ranking by user counts.
Shared analysis flagged manual steps as uncertain.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Release the full ranked pattern list and curation criteria, or provide an automated alternative (threshold, statistical selection) and compare extraction yield/precision under both procedures; quantify how many tuples change under alternative thresholds.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing evaluation lacks key annotation quality metrics
concerns.description: The crowdsourced inter-topic judgments omit reporting inter-annotator agreement measures (e.g., Krippendorff's α), instruction clarity, and distributional properties of sampled pairs; worker filtering via only 20 gold pairs may be insufficient.
evidence: Section 4.3 reports 6–10 judgments per pair, gold-set filtering, and mean scores but not IAA or label distributions.
Shared analysis notes limited crowdsourcing detail.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report IAA (Krippendorff's α or Fleiss' κ), provide the exact instructions and gold examples used, increase gold item set if possible, and publish the annotated pair list to allow external validation and error analysis.

Manual curation favored frequent patterns and frequent topics, so dataset may overweight mainstream political topics and underrepresent fringe or nuanced stances; reported accuracy could be inflated by this selection.

evidence: Paper claims first study to model inter-topic preferences for unlimited targets on real-world data (Introduction, contributions).
Related work cites Bamman & Smith (2015) as one-dimensional latent work; current approach explicitly targets multi-dimensional latent spaces and large-scale data (Sec. 5).
uncertainty_flags: Novelty is sensitive to prior unsupervised stance or co-preference work that may not have been retrieved; practical impact depends on extraction precision and generalizability.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Components (hashtag bootstrapping, pattern-based extraction, ru,t normalization, MF using libmf) are well-known individually. The main novelty is their integration and scale rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic advance.

Hashtag-based weak supervision has precedent in sentiment/emotion extraction (Davidov et al. 2010; Qadir & Riloff 2014).
uncertainty_flags: While algorithmic steps are incremental, integrated application to inter-topic preferences could still yield novel insights if empirical validity is established.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident (interval spanning 0.15–0.85) in the assessed strengths and methodological concerns. The paper's operational pipeline and scale are clear (high confidence), but the lack of extraction precision metrics, limited evaluation details (CIs, IAA), and language-specific seeding generate substantive uncertainty about practical validity and generalizability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a pipeline to acquire inter-topic preference knowledge from a large Japanese Twitter corpus: (1) seed pro/con hashtag regexes to find users and topics; (2) induce and manually filter pro/con sentence patterns; (3) extract (user,topic,stance) tuples and aggregate to ru,t = (pro−con)/(pro+con); (4) apply low-rank matrix factorization (libmf) to the sparse R to obtain user/topic latent vectors; (5) evaluate sign-prediction on 5% held-out observed entries and assess topic-vector similarity against crowdsourced inter-topic preference judgments. Evidence in the manuscript supports that the pipeline yields a very large dataset (≈9.96M tuples, 273k users, 2.3k topics), that factorization yields reasonable reconstruction RMSE decreasing with k (authors choose k=100), achieves high sign-prediction accuracy on held-out observed entries (82.1% for users with ≥5 known topics to 94% for ≥100), and that cosine similarity of topic vectors has a modest positive correlation (Spearman ρ≈0.221) with human judgments. Key weaknesses in the evidentiary chain are: (a) absence of sampled precision/recall or error analysis of pattern-based extraction, (b) ru,t construction and treatment of low-count/noisy cells not thoroughly validated, (c) evaluation restricted to predicting held-out observed cells (not cold-start users/topics) with no confidence intervals or repeated splits, (d) choice of k justified only by RMSE curve with no formal model-selection or downstream-task tuning, and (e) limited crowdsourcing detail and modest correlation for inter-topic judgments. I mark supported vs partially supported vs overstated claims in the identified_claims below and give specific, evidence-based suggestions and uncertainty flags.

Apply pro/con patterns to corpus → extract (u,t,v) tuples → aggregate counts per user-topic → compute ru,t ∈ [-1, +1]

Form sparse user×topic matrix R (only filled elements) → apply low-rank matrix factorization (libmf) minimizing squared error + L2 regularization over observed entries → obtain user vectors pu and topic vectors qt
Use puᵀqt to (a) predict sign(r_u,t) for held-out observed entries (5% random holdout) and (b) compute cosine similarity between topic vectors to identify inter-topic preference relations
Evaluate (a) prediction accuracy stratified by user vocality (θ known preferences) and (b) topic-vector alignment with human judgments via crowdsourcing (450 pairs stratified by cosine similarity)

identified_claims.claim_text: User-topic preference values ru,t can be computed as (#pro - #con)/(#pro + #con) producing values in [-1,+1] that represent degree of expressed preference.
evidence: Equation 1 defines ru,t = (#(u,t,+1) - #(u,t,-1)) / (#(u,t,+1) + #(u,t,-1)).
uncertainty_flags: No discussion of smoothing, minimum-count thresholds effect on ru,t, or how single-occurrence noisy matches are handled.
Temporal dynamics and contradictory expressions by same user not considered.

identified_claims.claim_text: Modeling the sparse user-topic matrix with low-rank matrix factorization yields user and topic latent vectors that can predict missing user-topic preferences with high accuracy (82.1% when ≥5 known preferences; 94.0% when ≥100).
evidence: Objective and optimization with libmf described (Eq.2).
Evaluation: 5% random held-out observed entries as test set (Section 4.2).
Reported sign-prediction accuracies: 82.1% for users with ≥5 known topics; 94.0% for users with ≥100 known topics (Figure 3).
uncertainty_flags: Evaluation only holds out observed entries for in-sample users/topics; does not measure cold-start or generalization to new users/topics.
No confidence intervals, variance across multiple random splits, or statistical tests reported.
Potential selection/leakage in train/test split not fully specified (random seed, repeats).

identified_claims.claim_text: Latent topic vectors capture meaningful inter-topic preference relations, as shown by qualitative nearest-neighbor examples and a moderate positive correlation (Spearman ρ≈0.221) with crowd judgments.
evidence: Crowdsourced evaluation: 450 topic pairs sampled by cosine similarity ranges; human labels mapped to {-1,0,+1} and averaged.
Spearman's ρ between cosine similarity and averaged human judgments reported as 0.221.
Nearest-neighbor topic lists for controversial topics (Table 2) show plausible related topics.
uncertainty_flags: Correlation is modest (ρ=0.221) — substantial unexplained variance.
Crowdsourcing details are limited: inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and full instructions not reported.
Sampling pairs stratified by cosine similarity can bias evaluation toward model-aligned pairs.

identified_claims.claim_text: A multi-dimensional latent space (k>1, e.g., k=100) is necessary; a single liberal–conservative axis (k=1) is insufficient to represent the diversity of topic preferences.
evidence: RMSE decreases as k increases; k=1 yields relatively high RMSE (Figure 2).
Authors choose k=100 as sufficient for reconstruction and use it in experiments.
uncertainty_flags: Choice of k=100 justified by RMSE curve but lacks held-out validation or downstream-task tuning; possible under/overfitting not quantified.
RMSE improvements continue up to k=500 (lowest reported RMSE), suggesting k=100 may be heuristic.

identified_claims.claim_text: The matrix factorization approach helps complete preferences for 'ordinary' (less vocal) users, bridging the gap between vocal and ordinary users.
evidence: Cites Cohen and Ruths (2013) regarding failures of prior methods on ordinary users.
Prediction accuracy improves with the number of known preferences, and authors argue latent completion benefits ordinary users.
Figure 4 shows variance of ru,t increases for more vocal users, suggesting vocal users deviate from average.
uncertainty_flags: No direct evaluation on cold-start or zero-observed users (the real 'ordinary' case).
Assumes latent factors learned primarily from vocal users generalize to ordinary users; not empirically validated.

strengths.title: Large-scale operational dataset construction
strengths.description: The paper demonstrates extraction of nearly 10M (u,t,v) tuples over 273k users and 2.3k topics from a 35M+ Japanese tweet corpus, showing practical throughput and scalability.
evidence: Reported final dataset: 9,961,509 tuples, 273,417 users, 2,323 topics (Sec.2.2).
Initial hashtag seed produced 31,068 occurrences and 4,899 topics (Sec.2.1).

strengths.title: Simple, interpretable pipeline linking linguistic patterns to latent modeling
strengths.description: The pipeline (hashtag-seed → pattern induction/filtering → tuple extraction → ru,t normalization → matrix factorization) is conceptually clear and maps to recommender-system techniques.
evidence: Clear description of seeding regexes, pattern extraction and manual filtering, ru,t definition (Eq.1), and matrix factorization objective (Eq.2).

strengths.title: Empirical demonstration of predictive utility
strengths.description: Held-out sign-prediction accuracy shows that the factorization recovers users' declared stances with high accuracy for sufficiently vocal users (82–94%).
evidence: Figure 3 and text: 82.1% accuracy for users with ≥5 known topics, 94.0% for ≥100 known topics.

strengths.title: Multiple complementary evaluations
strengths.description: The authors use reconstruction RMSE, held-out sign-prediction, qualitative nearest neighbors, and crowdsourced human judgments to probe different aspects of the model.
evidence: Sections 4.1 (RMSE/k selection), 4.2 (prediction), 4.3 (crowdsourcing + qualitative examples).

concerns.title: No sampled precision/recall or error analysis for pattern-based extraction
concerns.description: The central dataset (u,t,v) is produced by pattern matching seeded from hashtags and manual filtering, but no sampled precision (false positives) or recall (coverage) estimates are reported. Without such validation, ru,t values and downstream factorization may be biased by unknown noise levels (e.g., sarcasm, quoting, negation scope, false topical matches).
evidence: Shared analysis and manuscript report counts and manual filtering steps but do not report any sampled annotation of extracted tuples or error modes.
Assumptions A1, A2, A3 in shared analysis flag these risks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Randomly sample extracted (u,t,v) tuples (stratified by topic frequency and by pro/con) and annotate whether the extraction is correct; report precision, typical false-positive categories, and an estimate of recall via targeted retrieval or manual inspection of users with hashtag signals. Optionally, report extraction precision after automated pattern-filtering heuristics to reduce subjectivity.

concerns.title: ru,t brittle for low counts and unlabeled noise
concerns.description: The ru,t normalization treats small-count cells identically to high-count cells. Single or few noisy matches can yield extreme ru,t values which can distort factorization and prediction. No smoothing, minimum-count thresholds analysis, or robustness checks are provided.
evidence: Equation 1 defines ru,t as normalized difference with no smoothing.
Data cleaning removed users and topics with fewer than 5 appearances but per-(u,t) counts distribution and prevalence of single-occurrence cells are not reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report distribution of per-(u,t) counts; evaluate alternatives (e.g., add-one smoothing, Bayesian shrinkage toward 0, weight observations by count in factorization, or filter ru,t cells with counts below thresholds). Show effect on RMSE and prediction accuracy.

concerns.title: Evaluation limited to in-sample held-out entries with no uncertainty estimates
concerns.description: Prediction experiments randomly hold out 5% of observed entries but do not report multiple splits, confidence intervals, or performance on cold-start users/topics (zero observed entries). This makes reported point accuracies potentially optimistic and non-generalizable.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes a single random 5% holdout and reports point accuracies across vocality thresholds.
Shared analysis notes absence of repeated splits and CI reporting.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run repeated cross-validation (multiple random holdouts) and report mean ± standard error or 95% CIs. Evaluate cold-start performance: (a) users with zero training observations (train on other users), (b) new topics (leave-one-topic-out), and (c) transfer learning scenarios. Clarify random seed and splitting protocol for reproducibility.

concerns.title: k selection and overfitting not rigorously justified
concerns.description: The dimension k is chosen (k=100) based on RMSE curves on the entire observed data without held-out validation or downstream-task-driven selection; higher k up to 500 gives lower RMSE. No regularization tuning or checks for overfitting (e.g., test RMSE vs train RMSE) are described.
evidence: Section 4.1 shows RMSE decreasing with k and states k=100 is sufficient; lowest RMSE at k=500 reported.
Regularization λP,Q fixed to 0.1 without reported tuning.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Use held-out validation to pick k and λ, report train vs validation RMSE, and show downstream effects (prediction accuracy and topic-vector correlation) as a function of k. Report computational trade-offs and whether increasing k yields diminishing returns or overfitting.

concerns.title: Inter-topic evaluation has limited detail and modest correlation
concerns.description: Crowdsourced evaluation yields a modest Spearman ρ=0.221 between cosine similarity and averaged human judgments. However, worker instructions, inter-annotator agreement, and the potential bias from stratified sampling by model scores are not fully reported, limiting interpretation of the result.
evidence: Section 4.3 reports 450 pairs stratified by cosine similarity and a ρ of 0.221; IAA and full instructions not provided.
Shared analysis flags possible bias from sampling by cosine similarity ranges.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report annotation instructions, inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α or Fleiss’ κ), per-range agreement, and the distribution of human labels. Evaluate alternative association measures (e.g., conditional co-occurrence, PMI) as baselines and compute correlation to show added value of topic-vector cosine. Use random sampling of topic pairs (not stratified) or report results on both.

concerns.title: Generality beyond Japanese hashtag morphology untested
concerns.description: The method relies on Japanese hashtag conventions (#<topic>sansei/#<topic>hantai) and specific pattern boundary heuristics; claims of language-agnostic applicability are unverified.
evidence: Paper explicitly uses Japanese dataset and notes that approach is applicable to any language but provides no cross-lingual experiments.
Assumptions A3 and A10 in shared analysis highlight language/community specificity risks.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a small-scale experiment or discussion applying the seeding/pattern approach to an English Twitter sample (e.g., #X4Trump/#StopX patterns, or hashtag seeds like #Xsupport/#Xoppose) or describe how to adapt the pipeline across languages. At minimum, discuss limitations more explicitly.

comparable_works.relevance: Unsupervised latent modeling of political propositions with a one-dimensional latent axis; closely related in mapping subjects and users to latent space without labeled data.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar goal of unsupervised stance/ideology mapping, but Bamman & Smith aim for a 1D political spectrum via a generative model; current paper uses observed ru,t and explicit matrix factorization excluding missing entries, and argues for multi-dimensional structure.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature and manuscript Related Work (Section 5)

comparable_works.relevance: Matrix factorization for recommendation; methodological precedent and justification for low-rank user/item latent factors.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Methodological match: applying MF to user×item (user×topic) sparse matrix. Difference: labels here are normalized stance values ([-1,+1]) rather than ratings.

comparable_works.relevance: Use of hashtags as distant supervision for sentiment/emotion; provides precedent for hashtag seeding.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar seeding idea; current paper exploits language-specific pro/con morphological suffixes and manual pattern induction at scale.

comparable_works.relevance: Difficulty of stance detection on ordinary users versus vocal users; motivates utility of completion for less-vocal users.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Provides motivation; current paper attempts to bridge vocal/ordinary gap via latent completion but lacks direct cold-start validation.

comparable_works.relevance: State-of-art stance detection benchmarks showing cross-topic difficulty; situates the need for inter-topic knowledge.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: SemEval focuses on supervised stance per topic; current work aims to learn cross-topic relations unsupervised from pattern-extracted counts.

uncertainty_flags: No sampled precision/recall for extraction (major uncertainty about input data quality).
ru,t values can be unstable for low counts—no smoothing or sensitivity checks reported.
Prediction evaluation uses in-sample held-out entries only; cold-start generalization unknown.
Reported prediction accuracies are point estimates without CIs or repeated splits.
Inter-topic correlation with human judgments is modest (ρ=0.221); crowdsourcing reliability metrics not reported.
Choice of k and regularization not selected via held-out validation; k=100 is heuristic.
alternative_interpretations: High sign-prediction accuracy for vocal users may mainly reflect redundancy in labels: users who comment on many topics may use consistent language patterns that the model easily reconstructs, rather than latent factors capturing genuine ideological coherence applicable to ordinary users.

Topic-vector cosine similarity may partly capture topical or lexical similarity (shared vocabulary in extracted patterns) rather than pure co-preference; cosine could be conflated with semantic relatedness or co-occurrence frequency.

Moderate correlation with human judgments could indicate that model captures a subset of inter-topic relations (e.g., strong partisan policy clusters) but not nuanced or context-dependent associations.
The high dataset size may mask heavy class imbalance: a large number of low-count or auto-generated tweets could dominate factorization unless counts and weights are managed.
transparency_notes: Authors should release a sampled gold set of extracted (u,t,v) tuples and pattern lists to enable reproduction and external audit of extraction precision.
Details for the experimental protocol (random seed, number of repeats, train/validation/test splits) are missing and should be included for reproducibility.
Crowdsourcing instructions, qualification criteria, and inter-annotator agreement metrics should be reported to assess the reliability of human judgments.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The combination of hashtag-seeded pattern induction at massive scale with matrix factorization to derive inter-topic preference embeddings appears distinct from close prior works. However, novelty in approach does not guarantee validity: core empirical claims hinge on the unvalidated extraction pipeline and evaluation methodology.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If pattern-based extraction precision is high (e.g., >90%) after manual filtering, then ru,t values are reliable inputs and factorization predictions/embeddings are meaningful.
If per-(u,t) counts are sufficiently large for most filled cells, ru,t instability is reduced and latent factors reflect genuine preference structure.
If multiple random splits and held-out validation confirm stable prediction accuracy with narrow confidence intervals, claims about predictive performance generalize.
If crowdsourced judgments show acceptable inter-annotator agreement and correlation stays or improves with better annotation, then topic-vector similarity plausibly encodes inter-topic preference.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Applying matrix factorization to user×topic stance matrices extends well-known recommender-system techniques to a novel label construction (pattern-extracted ru,t) at large scale. The novelty is incremental in method (MF applied to a different signal) but contributes novel empirical scale and operational extraction.
evidence: Use of libmf and MF follows established recommender literature (Koren et al.).
Extraction pipeline (hashtag-seed → pattern induction → ru,t) is an operational adaptation of hashtag distant supervision literature.
uncertainty_flags: Depends on whether extraction quality and cross-topic generalization are demonstrated; if extraction is noisy, methodological novelty loses practical impact.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If the extraction pipeline reliably builds large, high-quality ru,t matrices across many domains, the approach could enable cross-topic stance inference and multi-axis opinion modeling beyond single-axis political spectra—this would be a disruptive capability for computational social science. However, lack of extraction validation and generalization experiments leaves disruptive potential unproven.
evidence: Authors claim first modeling of inter-topic preferences for unlimited targets on real-world data.
Large-scale dataset and end-to-end pipeline could scale to new domains.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical validation gaps (precision, cold-start, cross-lingual transfer) must be closed before disruption is substantiated.

confidence_interval.rationale: I provide qualitative confidence descriptors for individual findings above (high/medium/low). The overall confidence in the paper's main empirical claims is conditional: the numerical results reported (dataset sizes, RMSE trends, point accuracies, and reported correlation) are likely accurate as presented in the manuscript. However, confidence in broader generalizations (dataset quality, applicability to ordinary users and other languages, and robustness of inter-topic embeddings) is substantially lower because key validation steps and uncertainty quantification are missing. Thus, a numerical CI is not meaningful; the provided lower/upper bounds indicate that conclusions range from fully supported given additional evidence to unsupported if extraction is noisy.

consensus_findings: The pipeline is clearly described and scale is substantial: authors extract a very large (≈9.96M) set of (user,topic,stance) tuples from a large Japanese Twitter crawl and apply low-rank matrix factorization (libmf) to the resulting sparse user×topic matrix.

Matrix factorization on the constructed ru,t matrix produces latent user and topic vectors that achieve high in-sample sign-prediction accuracy on held-out observed entries, with accuracy rising as the number of known preferences per user increases.

Topic latent vectors exhibit some alignment with human judgments of inter-topic preference: qualitative nearest-neighbor examples are plausible and a modest positive Spearman correlation (reported ρ≈0.221) was observed between cosine similarity and crowdsourced association judgments.

Several methodological and reporting gaps are consistently noted by reviewers: lack of sampled precision/recall for the pattern-extraction pipeline, sensitivity of ru,t to low counts and lack of smoothing, evaluation limited to held-out observed entries (no cold-start tests), heuristic k selection without held-out validation, and incomplete crowdsourcing reporting (IAA, instructions, sampling effects).
disagreements: Degree-of-concern about novelty: some reviewers emphasize the contribution as meaningful incremental engineering at scale (integration of known methods), while others emphasize conceptual novelty (framing inter-topic preference acquisition as matrix completion) — both readings are supported by evidence but differ in emphasis.

Interpretation of high sign-prediction accuracy: one view interprets it as substantive evidence that latent factors capture co-preference structure; an alternative view argues much of the accuracy may be driven by majority-topic signals, frequent users, or redundancy in labels rather than generalizable latent structure.

Strength of evidence that topic vectors encode human-relevant inter-topic preference: reviewers agree on a positive signal but disagree whether the reported correlation (ρ≈0.221) and qualitative examples are strong enough to claim robust encoding beyond superficial topical/semantic similarity.
uncertainty_hotspots: Extraction quality of (u,t,v) tuples: no stratified sampled precision/recall or error-mode analysis reported (sarcasm, negation, quoting). This is the single largest empirical uncertainty affecting downstream claims.
Stability of ru,t values: many filled cells may have low counts; ru,t = (#+ - #-) / (#+ + #-) can be extreme for single occurrences and no smoothing/weighting analysis was reported.
Generalization beyond held-in-sample evaluation: reported predictive performance is on held-out observed entries for in-sample users/topics; performance for cold-start users or new topics is unknown.
Model-selection and overfitting: k=100 is chosen heuristically from RMSE; no held-out validation for k or regularization was reported and RMSE improvements extend up to larger k values.

Interpretation of topic-vector cosine: cosine similarity may conflate semantic/topical similarity with preference co-occurrence; stratified sampling by cosine in the crowdsourced evaluation may bias the correlation estimate.
Crowdsourcing reliability: inter-annotator agreement, exact instructions, construction of gold items, and per-pair variance are not reported, limiting confidence in the human-judgment benchmark.
model_diversity_effects: Different reviewer roles highlight complementary risks: structure/logic-focused reviewers flag possible alternative causal chains (e.g., majority-topic effects) whereas reproducibility auditors stress missing procedural details (seeds, seeds filtering, random seeds) that affect replicability of results.

Methodology-oriented reviewers emphasize the need to treat missingness and low-count uncertainty (statistical weighting, smoothing, cold-start) — changes here could materially alter reported accuracies and the semantic structure of topic vectors.

Novelty-assessing reviewers disagree on framing (incremental engineering vs conceptually novel framing), which affects perceived contribution value but not the empirical gaps; this diversity signals that the paper's impact is sensitive to how convincingly empirical validity and generalizability are demonstrated.

Operational choices (manual pattern curation, frequency thresholds, ru,t transform, sampling for crowdsourcing) are likely to produce different downstream latent spaces; thus, small methodological variations could create qualitatively different topic embeddings and predictive behavior.
meta_review.editor_guidance: The editor should treat the manuscript as offering an interesting, large-scale pipeline with promising preliminary results but with critical validation gaps that need to be addressed before stronger claims are accepted. Key items for the authors to provide (or for reviewers to re-evaluate after revision) are: (1) sampled precision and error-mode analysis of the extracted (u,t,v) tuples (stratified by frequency and pattern type); (2) robustness analyses for ru,t (distribution of per-cell counts, smoothing/weighting experiments, effect on downstream metrics); (3) expanded evaluation including repeated random splits with confidence intervals and explicit cold-start experiments (entire users/topics held out); (4) model-selection via held-out validation for k and regularization and ablation of downstream metrics vs k; (5) full crowdsourcing reporting (instructions, gold items, inter-annotator agreement, per-pair variance) and correlation analyses using uniformly sampled pairs and baseline association measures (PMI, conditional co-occurrence). The editor may prioritize these reproducibility and robustness checks over stylistic changes. Preserve the authors' dataset contribution while requiring stronger quantification of data quality and generalization before endorsing broader claims about societal applicability or language-agnostic transfer.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidentiary support and reduce epistemic uncertainty, please provide the following in a revision: (A) Extraction validation: release or report a stratified manual annotation of extracted (u,t,v) tuples (e.g., 1,000+ samples across pro/con and high/low-frequency topics), report precision, catalog common failure modes (sarcasm, negation, quoting), and provide the full ranked pattern list and criteria used for manual filtering. (B) ru,t robustness: report distribution of per-(u,t) counts, fraction of cells at extreme ±1, and rerun core experiments with one or more alternative ru,t treatments (Laplace/Beta smoothing, count-weighted loss, or Bayesian shrinkage); show impacts on RMSE and sign-accuracy. (C) Evaluation rigor: perform repeated random hold-out or k-fold experiments and report mean ± standard error or 95% CIs; include cold-start experiments where entire users and/or topics are held out from training to test generalization. (D) Model selection: select k and regularization using a held-out validation set and report downstream metrics (sign-accuracy, topic-cosine correlation) vs k to show saturation or trade-offs. (E) Inter-topic validation: provide full crowdsourcing materials, report inter-annotator agreement statistics, rerun correlation analyses on uniformly sampled topic pairs and compare to simple baselines (co-occurrence, PMI) to demonstrate added value of topic vectors. (F) Transparency: disclose random seeds, libmf hyperparameters, and (if privacy permits) release anonymized sampled extraction outputs and the pattern list to enable external audit. Addressing these will materially strengthen claims and interpretability.
transparency_report: Manuscript provides a clear end-to-end pipeline description (hashtag regex seeds, pattern induction, ru,t formula, matrix factorization objective and tool).

Omitted reproducibility details: ranked pattern lists and explicit manual-filtering criteria, list of removed 'meaningless' topics, random seeds and number of factorization runs, full libmf hyperparameter grid and final training logs.
Omitted annotation reporting: crowdsourcing instructions, gold-pair examples, worker qualification/filtering statistics, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and per-pair judgment variance.
Evaluation reporting gaps: single reported random 5% holdout without repeats or confidence intervals, no cold-start experiments, and heuristic selection of k without held-out validation.
Data release status unclear: reviewers request a sampled annotated gold set and pattern lists to permit independent verification.
epistemic_limits: Current evidence supports that the pipeline can produce a large ru,t matrix and that low-rank factorization can reconstruct held-in-sample entries with high sign-agreement. However, the degree to which these results generalize beyond the extracted, hashtag-using population is uncertain because missingness is likely non-random and extraction noise is unquantified. The interpretation of topic-vector cosine as capturing human-interpretable inter-topic preference relations is only partly supported (modest correlation and limited annotation reporting). Therefore, inferences about (a) applicability to ordinary (zero- or low-activity) users, (b) robustness across languages/platforms, and (c) the semantic/causal meaning of latent dimensions remain provisional until (i) extraction precision/recall and error modes are quantified, (ii) ru,t robustness and smoothing are tested, (iii) generalization is evaluated including cold-start scenarios, and (iv) topic-vector validation is strengthened with better crowdsourcing and baseline comparisons. These are necessary to move from promising pilot-scale evidence to credible, generalizable claims.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript presents a pipeline that (1) seeds pattern induction with pro/con Japanese hashtags to extract large-scale (user, topic, stance) tuples, (2) aggregates counts into normalized ru,t values, and (3) applies low-rank matrix factorization (libmf) to complete missing user-topic stances and produce topic embeddings. Experiments report a final dataset of ~9.96M tuples (273k users × 2.3k topics), RMSE curves used to pick k (k=100), held-in-sample sign-prediction accuracy rising from ≈82% (users with ≥5 known topics) to ≈94% (≥100), qualitative nearest-neighbor topic lists, and a crowdsourced correlation (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.221) between topic-vector cosine similarity and averaged human judgments.
strengths: Clear, reproducible-seeming pipeline linking hashtag seeding → pattern induction → ru,t aggregation → scalable matrix factorization (libmf), described with formal equations (Eq.1, Eq.2).

Large-scale operational dataset: authors report nearly 10M extracted tuples across hundreds of thousands of users and thousands of topics, demonstrating practical throughput and engineering integration.

Complementary evaluations: reconstruction RMSE, held-in-sample sign-prediction stratified by user vocality, qualitative nearest-neighbor examples, and a human-judgment crowdsourced probe of topic-vector association.
limitations: No sampled precision/recall or error-mode analysis for the extracted (user,topic,stance) tuples. The extraction pipeline is central; without stratified annotation (e.g., pro/con correctness across frequency bins) the noise rate and dominant failure modes (sarcasm, negation, quoting, topical mismatch) are unknown, undermining confidence in ru,t inputs and downstream results.

ru,t computation and low-count handling are under-specified. ru,t = (#pro - #con)/(#pro + #con) yields extreme ±1 values for single-occurrence cells; the manuscript lacks distributional statistics of per-(u,t) counts and no smoothing or uncertainty-weighting experiments are reported, raising the possibility that noisy singletons materially influence factorization.

Evaluation protocol concentrates on held-out observed entries for in-sample users/topics (single random 5% holdout) with no repeats, confidence intervals, or cold-start tests. Generalization to zero-observed users or unseen topics is untested, yet claims about helping 'ordinary' users depend on such transfer.

Topic-vector validation is limited and possibly biased: crowdsourced sampling stratified by model cosine ranges and modest reported correlation (ρ≈0.221) leave open whether cosine captures co-preference vs simple topical/lexical similarity; inter-annotator agreement and full annotation materials are not reported.
open_questions: Please report a stratified manual annotation (e.g., ≥1,000 sampled tuples across pro/con and high/low-frequency topics): what are precision and (if estimable) recall for extracted stance labels, and what are the dominant error categories (sarcasm, negation, quotation, topical mismatch)?

What is the distribution of per-(u,t) counts and proportion of cells at ±1? Please show sensitivity analyses: (a) ru,t with Laplace/Bayesian smoothing or count-weighting in the loss, and (b) impact of these alternatives on RMSE and held-in-sample sign-prediction accuracy.

Provide evaluation robustness: rerun prediction experiments with multiple random splits or k-fold cross-validation, report mean ± standard error or 95% CI for accuracy/RMSE, and include cold-start experiments where entire users (or topics) are held out at train time—how do results change?

For topic-vector validation, provide full crowdsourcing materials and statistics (instructions, gold items, worker filtering thresholds, inter-annotator agreement such as Krippendorff's α or Fleiss' κ) and compare cosine-based similarity to baseline association measures (e.g., user co-agreement PMI or conditional co-occurrence).
consensus_snapshot: Reviewers agree the pipeline is well-described and the dataset scale is substantial (~9.96M tuples, 273k users, 2.3k topics).
Matrix factorization reconstructs held-in-sample entries with high sign-agreement, and predictive accuracy increases with number of known preferences per user.

Topic latent vectors show some alignment with human judgments (qualitative examples and a modest positive Spearman correlation ≈0.221), but confidence in this alignment is limited by evaluation design.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers emphasize the work as meaningful incremental engineering at scale (integration of known techniques), while others view the framing of inter-topic preference acquisition as conceptually novel; these perspectives differ but both note that empirical validation is the key determinant of impact.

Interpretation of high sign-prediction accuracy: some interpret it as substantive evidence of learned co-preference structure; others caution that accuracy may be driven by strong majority-topic signals, frequent users, or label redundancy rather than generalizable latent structure.

Degree to which topic-vector cosine captures preference (vs topical/lexical similarity): reviewers agree on a positive signal but disagree whether the reported correlation and qualitative examples establish robust encoding of inter-topic preference.
uncertainty_snapshot: Largest epistemic uncertainty stems from unlabeled input quality: absence of extraction precision/recall quantification directly threatens downstream inferences.
Uncertainty about ru,t stability for low-count cells and the effect of alternative aggregations/smoothing on factorization outcomes.
Uncertainty about generalization beyond vocal, hashtag-using users (non-random missingness) and to other languages/platforms (pipeline tuned to Japanese hashtag morphology).
Uncertainty in topic-vector interpretation due to modest crowd correlation, stratified sampling design, and missing annotator-agreement metrics.
source_trace: Bamman, D. & Smith, N. (2015). Prior work on unsupervised latent political spaces; cited as conceptual precedent in manuscript (Section 5).
Koren, Y. et al. (2009). Matrix factorization foundations in recommender systems; methodological basis for low-rank factorization approach (Section 3).
Davidov, D. et al. (2010). Use of hashtags as distant supervision for sentiment in tweets; supports hashtag seeding rationale (Section 2.1).
Cohen, S. & Ruths, D. (2013). Demonstrates difficulty of applying models trained on vocal users to ordinary users; manuscript cites as motivation for completion (Introduction).
libmf (Chin et al., 2015). Identified implementation used for scalable matrix factorization; manuscript states use of libmf and regularization choices (Section 3).
transparency_notes: Manuscript gives clear pipeline description and equations (ru,t, factorization objective) and reports dataset counts and main hyperparameters (e.g., λ = 0.1). Missing reproducibility artifacts: ranked pattern lists and the exact manual-filtering choices (which patterns/topics were removed), random seeds and number of runs for factorization, full libmf parameter settings and training logs, crowdsourcing instructions and gold items, inter-annotator agreement statistics, and release status of a sampled annotated gold set. Providing these will substantially improve transparency and external auditability.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the submission as promising and engineering-scale but incomplete in empirical validation. Prioritize requests that materially affect core claims: require stratified annotation-based precision estimates for extraction; robustness checks for ru,t (smoothing/weighting) and re-run of downstream experiments; repeated-split reporting with confidence intervals; cold-start/generalization experiments; and complete crowdsourcing documentation (instructions, golds, IAA). If authors supply these analyses and address selection/missingness concerns, re-evaluation should focus on whether corrected/robust results sustain the claimed contributions.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the evidentiary chain, please (1) provide a stratified manual annotation of extracted (u,t,v) tuples (report precision and common error modes); (2) report per-(u,t) count distributions and rerun key experiments with smoothed ru,t (e.g., add-α/Beta shrinkage) or count-weighted loss and report effects on RMSE and sign-accuracy; (3) run repeated random-split or k-fold evaluations and report mean ± SE / 95% CIs, and include cold-start tests (entire users/topics held out) to assess generalization; (4) select k and regularization via a held-out validation set and show downstream metrics vs k; (5) provide full crowdsourcing materials, inter-annotator agreement, per-pair variance, and comparisons of topic-vector cosine against baseline association measures (PMI, co-occurrence). Release or attach the pattern lists and a sampled annotated gold set if privacy permits.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper introduces a scalable pipeline that seeds pattern induction from Japanese pro/con hashtags to extract large (user,topic,stance) tuples, aggregates them via a normalized ru,t formula, and applies low-rank matrix factorization (libmf) to complete missing stances and to produce topic embeddings. Reported outcomes include nearly 10M tuples, RMSE-driven dimensional choice (k=100), strong held-in-sample sign-prediction accuracy for sufficiently vocal users (≈82%–94%), and modest alignment (Spearman ρ≈0.221) between topic-vector cosine and averaged human judgments.

Strengths:
- Well-specified end-to-end pipeline with formalization (Eq.1, Eq.2) and use of scalable MF (libmf).
- Substantial engineering and dataset scale enabling wide empirical exploration (~9.96M tuples, 273k users, 2.3k topics).
- Multiple evaluation angles (RMSE, held-in-sample prediction, qualitative neighbors, crowdsourced human judgments).

Limitations:
- No sampled precision/recall or error-mode analysis for extracted (u,t,v) tuples; the lack of labeled checks means ru,t inputs may have unknown noise that could bias all downstream results.
- ru,t is brittle for low-count cells (singletons yield ±1) and the manuscript omits per-cell count distributions and smoothing/weighting alternatives; this threatens factorization stability.
- Evaluation confined to held-out observed entries without repeated splits, CIs, or cold-start experiments—claims on generalization (esp. to 'ordinary' users or new topics) are not empirically supported.
- Topic-vector validation is limited: crowdsourcing sampling stratified by cosine and missing IAA statistics make the reported ρ≈0.221 hard to interpret as robust evidence that embeddings capture inter-topic preference rather than topical/lexical similarity.

- How accurate are the extracted stances? Provide stratified manual annotation results (precision; preferred sample sizes and stratification scheme noted above) and enumerate common failure modes (sarcasm, negation, quoting).
- What fraction of per-(u,t) cells are singletons or low-count? Please report the count distribution and re-evaluate experiments using smoothed ru,t (e.g., add-α or Bayesian shrinkage) or weight-by-count in the loss—how do RMSE and sign-accuracy change?
- Can you present repeated-split/k-fold evaluation with mean ± SE or 95% CIs for the sign-prediction and RMSE results, and include cold-start tests where entire users or topics are held out during training?
- For the crowdsourced inter-topic test, please release the full instructions, gold items, worker-filtering rules, inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's α or Fleiss' κ), and rerun correlations on both stratified and uniformly random topic-pair samples and against baseline association measures (PMI/co-occurrence).

Transparency:
The manuscript explains the pipeline and main hyperparameters but omits critical reproducibility artifacts: (a) ranked pattern lists and the exact manual curation criteria, (b) list of removed/top-100 'meaningless' topics, (c) random seeds and number of MF runs, (d) full libmf parameterization and training logs, (e) crowdsourcing instructions and IAA statistics, and (f) a sampled annotated gold set of extracted tuples. Providing these will materially increase reproducibility and allow auditors to evaluate the core data quality assumptions.
